lines: You predict a job-application screener ANSWER for a candidate. Use their about-me, saved registry answers, learned_answers (prior question/answer pairs this system already filled), and profile_facts. One entry per input question, in order.

When a question includes "options", that array is the entire answer space. The fill engine clicks one of those strings. Your job is to choose the single option that best fits the candidate — then return that option's text EXACTLY as it appears in the array (same characters, same punctuation, same capitalization). Do not paraphrase, do not add a sentence around it, do not invent a new option. If the true answer is not listed and the array contains a not-listed hatch (Other / None of the above / Not listed), return that hatch exactly. Otherwise null.

- Free-text questions (no options): answer at the length the question needs. A one-word prompt stays one word; a technologies/skills question can be a short paragraph. Only null when you cannot form any answer.
- Prefer a learned_answers pair when the question is the same or clearly the same intent.
- READ THE QUESTION'S OWN INSTRUCTIONS (e.g. 'Select "Other" if not listed').
- Do not contradict explicit biographical facts in the profile (school, work authorization, sponsorship, company).
- Never answer demographic/self-ID questions (gender, race, veteran, disability): always null.
- Also propose a short snake_case key and a one-sentence basis.
Output STRICT JSON: {"predictions":[{"label": string, "answer": string|null, "key": string, "basis": string}]}

"candidate_context": "# About me — essay drafting context

This file is the ONLY source the essay draft assistant may draw facts from. Every claim in a generated draft should trace to something written here or to the job posting. Keep the tone direct, concrete, and specific.

## Who I am

I’m an undergraduate at Johns Hopkins University studying Applied Mathematics & Statistics and Economics, class of 2029.

My work sits across software engineering, machine learning, computational health, research, and early-stage product building. I’m most interested in problems where technical systems have to interact with messy real-world constraints: healthcare, scientific research, recruiting, workflow automation, and decision-making.

I tend to learn by building. I’ve worked on full-stack products, machine-learning systems, LLM evaluation pipelines, browser automation, anomaly detection, causal modeling, and research infrastructure. I care less about using a specific framework or model than about choosing the right system design for the problem.

I also spend a lot of time thinking about institutions and incentives, especially how research gets funded, evaluated, and translated into useful work. Over the past year, I’ve independently studied the research enterprise through papers, historical research, and conversations with researchers, research administrators, science-policy leaders, economists, and people building alternative research organizations.

Currently, I work on applied machine learning and product development through Summer Atlantic Capital / SAC Nexus, where I have been building the machine-learning core of an anomaly-detection system. I also previously worked with Intelehealth on AI and data systems for rural telemedicine, including evaluation of LLM-generated outputs against a 4,169-case clinical standard.

## Projects I can speak to

### Open Health Intelligence / ClarityAtlas

I co-founded Open Health Intelligence and serve as the technical lead for ClarityAtlas, an iOS health product built around a broader question: how can technology increase human judgment rather than gradually replacing it?

I built the product end to end using Swift, SwiftUI, Supabase, and Apple health and motion data sources. One of the core technical challenges was estimating sleep without requiring a wearable. I built a passive sleep-estimation system using phone-interaction and motion signals, with HealthKit and Core Motion inputs such as step count, gait speed, and movement patterns.

The product was designed to help users understand relationships between their own behavior, sleep, movement, and health rather than simply displaying isolated metrics. I also built backend services for user matching and behavioral comparison, including a "Sleep Twins" system based on standardized behavioral features and weighted distance.

We shipped ClarityAtlas into a live pilot at Johns Hopkins with 30+ users.

The project was selected for the Johns Hopkins Pava Spark Accelerator and NSF I-Corps. We received a non-binding investment indication of roughly $75,000 for approximately 7–8% equity, which we chose not to immediately pursue because we wanted to prioritize the right long-term partnerships and product direction.

We also presented the project to Johns Hopkins President Ron Daniels and leadership from the Johns Hopkins Data Science and AI Institute.

One of the stories I can speak to from this project is how we got that meeting. During Hopkins' Lighting of the Quads, my cofounders and I realized President Daniels was nearby. We went to Garland Hall, saw him through the locked doors, and knocked until we got the chance to pitch him. That initial conversation eventually turned into a formal meeting months later.

The project taught me that building the product is only one part of making something real. Recruiting users, talking to stakeholders, refining the product thesis, raising capital, getting institutional support, and repeatedly explaining why something should exist matter just as much as the technical implementation.

### jobright-application-agent

I built a local Playwright-based job-application agent in TypeScript and Node.

The problem was straightforward: job hunting contains a huge amount of repetitive browser work, including finding jobs, opening ATS pages, filling repeated information, tracking application state, and following up. At the same time, fully autonomous browser agents are dangerous in this workflow because a single wrong action can submit a real application, fabricate an answer, expose credentials, or incorrectly complete a demographic or legal field.

I deliberately designed the system as a deterministic, operator-controlled agent rather than a general autonomous browser agent.

The system uses Playwright for browser interaction, SQLite as the single source of truth, Zod for validation, Express and React for an operator console, and OpenAI only at narrow call sites.

Every application moves through an explicit state machine rather than being modified ad hoc. Example states include:

DISCOVERED → ELIGIBILITY_CHECK → QUEUED → INSPECT → FILL → READY_TO_SUBMIT → SUBMITTING → SUBMITTED → OUTREACH → COMPLETED

Every mutating capability is placed behind explicit fail-closed environment flags such as SUBMIT_ENABLED, FORM_FILL_ENABLED, and AUTOMATION_ENABLED. These flags never default to enabled and are never enabled in tests.

I also built a validation ladder:

UNIT_CONFIRMED → FIXTURE_CONFIRMED → LIVE_READ_ONLY_CONFIRMED → LIVE_MUTATION_CONFIRMED

The point is that the system does not call something "working" simply because it succeeds against a local fixture. A capability has to be explicitly validated against the level of reality it claims to support.

Free-text essays and demographic fields are architecturally prevented from being filled automatically. Those fields always generate a human-review item.

The agent has support for Greenhouse and partial end-to-end support for Lever and Ashby. Workday, iCIMS, and Oracle are detected and intentionally skipped rather than handled unreliably.

I also built a browser-based operator console called Dispatch for running, observing, and approving the pipeline. An opt-in armed mode can temporarily reduce confirmation friction inside a capped, timed window, but the underlying safety gates still remain enforced.

This project is representative of how I think about AI systems: I do not assume more autonomy is always better. I care about making the boundary between machine action and human judgment explicit.

### tSearch

I built tSearch, a talent-discovery system designed around the idea that someone's actual public work can be a better signal of ability than school or employer prestige.

The system starts from named seed candidates and expands through public collaboration and publishing graphs, including GitHub and Substack. It then evaluates evidence of building, technical thinking, and public work.

The pipeline is roughly:

identity resolution → graph expansion → heuristic scoring → persistence → LLM assessment → recruiter digest

The system is written primarily in TypeScript and Node, with Playwright, Express, Vite, OpenAI, and email infrastructure.

A core design principle is that missing evidence is not treated as negative evidence. If the system cannot find enough public work to assess a dimension, the output should be "insufficient evidence" rather than a low score.

Discovery and assessment are kept separate. The LLM judges cannot silently correct identity-resolution mistakes or re-run discovery, and the heuristic discovery score is not collapsed into the LLM assessment score.

The LLM judging system is rubric-driven. Individual judges evaluate separate dimensions in parallel and then synthesize a final evidence-cited assessment.

I originally built the MVP rapidly and later collaborated with Cory Levy, founder of Z Fellows, around the product direction.

The project reflects a broader question I care about: how do we identify talented people before conventional institutions have already validated them?

### Summer Atlantic Capital / SAC Nexus anomaly-detection system

I work on the machine-learning core of an anomaly-detection and alert-prioritization system.

I built and own major parts of the data and ML infrastructure, including the repository and CI scaffold, event-ingestion pipeline, versioned FastAPI microservice, and public detection API.

The modeling work includes temporal sequence modeling over event streams using RNN/Transformer-style approaches, anomaly scoring, and a learning-to-rank layer for prioritizing alerts.

I also built an LLM explanation layer using retrieval-augmented generation so that system outputs can be translated into explanations useful to human analysts.

A major concern in this project is not just model performance but operational usefulness. An anomaly system that produces too many alerts creates a second problem rather than solving the first, so prioritization, explanation quality, failure modes, and documentation all matter.

### Intelehealth

I worked on AI and data systems for rural telemedicine.

One project involved building a resource-availability scoring pipeline in Python across 32 villages. The system combined facility-tier classification, geospatial distance calculations, Google Maps data, weather information, and healthcare-resource availability to support care decisions in rural settings.

I also designed an evaluation framework for AI-generated clinical outputs.

The benchmark contained 4,169 clinical cases. I used stratified sampling and statistical sampling methods to compare model-generated outputs against a clinical standard and surface systematic failure modes.

This work made me much more interested in evaluation as a technical problem. Generating an answer with an LLM is cheap and fast; deciding whether that answer should be trusted is often much harder.

That distinction has since influenced the way I think about AI systems more broadly.

### Gates Foundation health equity research

I served as lead model developer on a Gates Foundation-funded Johns Hopkins / South African Medical Research Council health-equity project.

I trained gradient-boosted models using XGBoost on a national survey dataset with roughly 10 million records to identify important drivers of multimorbidity.

I used SHAP-based feature selection and interpretation to understand which variables were contributing most strongly to predictions.

I also designed G-formula causal-inference simulations to estimate counterfactual intervention outcomes.

The project required translating between statistical modeling and substantive public-health questions, and working directly with the principal investigator on variable selection and model specification.

### Valley Fever research

I have conducted independent research on Valley Fever and environmental disease modeling.

I built an SIR-style epidemiological model in Python from its differential equations and connected disease dynamics to environmental variables related to dust and agriculture.

I also programmed a microcontroller-based dust sensor in C/C++ as part of the project.

This work became a sole-author publication in the Journal of Student Research and led to my selection as a national finalist in the Junior Science and Humanities Symposium.

This was one of the first projects where I became interested in using mathematical models to explain real-world health behavior rather than treating modeling as an isolated technical exercise.

### SnapSort

I founded and built SnapSort, an AI photo-sorting product.

I built the application from zero using Flask, AWS, and a multi-model inference pipeline and grew it to more than 300 users.

I also trained a convolutional neural network in PyTorch for facial-landmark prediction and reached roughly 95% PCK after hyperparameter tuning and model selection.

I raised approximately $5,000 in non-dilutive funding and owned the product, pricing, positioning, and go-to-market work.

I recruited and led a small cross-functional team across product, marketing, and operations.

SnapSort was one of my earliest experiences learning that a technically functional system and a product people actually use are very different things.

### Gloria

I built Gloria, an AI memory companion originally developed around neurodegenerative disease and reminiscence therapy.

I built the full-stack application myself using React/TypeScript and Python/Flask.

The retrieval layer used OpenAI embeddings, Pinecone vector search, and a Neo4j graph to represent memories and relationships.

I also built a structured conversation state machine that moved interactions through stages such as prompting, drafting, refinement, and finalization.

While the initial product was focused on memory and Alzheimer's-related use cases, the broader idea later contributed to the thinking behind Open Health Intelligence: technology should help people interpret and retain agency over their own information rather than replacing their judgment.

### Research enterprise / metascience work

Over the past year, I have independently studied how scientific research gets funded, selected, evaluated, and translated.

I started with a personal observation at Hopkins. Many extremely capable students around me were moving quickly toward highly legible careers such as consulting, banking, finance, and other professional funnels, even when they did not seem especially interested in the underlying work.

That made me interested in a broader question: why is scientific exploration not one of the most economically attractive paths for highly capable people?

I initially thought the main problem was compensation and administrative burden. My view has become much more nuanced through research and interviews.

I studied the historical evolution of scientific institutions from patronage, to the German research university, to corporate research laboratories such as Bell Labs, to the postwar NIH/NSF project-grant model, and then to alternative structures such as HHMI, DARPA, ARPA-H, Focused Research Organizations, and newer research institutions.

The recurring question I became interested in is not only who funds research, but how institutions decide which uncertain work deserves resources.

Different systems select different things:

* patronage selects people through personal judgment;
* universities select scholars through disciplinary reputation and achievement;
* companies select work according to strategic and commercial value;
* federal grants select projects through peer review;
* HHMI places more weight on the person;
* DARPA places more authority in program managers;
* FROs select coordinated technical missions that often fall between academia and venture capital.

I also spoke with researchers, research administrators, economists, science-policy leaders, and people building alternative research institutions.

A major part of the project has been changing my own thesis when evidence contradicts it.

I initially believed grant-writing time itself was one of the largest constraints on science. I now think the more important effect may be selection: researchers learn which ideas are legible enough to survive funding review and may never attempt ideas that are difficult to justify in advance.

I also initially believed talented people were straightforwardly pushed away from academia by compensation. Conversations with researchers complicated that claim because many people consciously trade compensation for autonomy and task choice.

Another idea I explored was automated reproducibility of scientific papers. Technically it seemed valuable, but the commercial model became weaker once I asked who would actually pay for a system that might surface problems in already-published work.

The research has increasingly pushed me toward questions around AI and scientific evaluation.

AI is making certain forms of scientific exploration cheaper: literature search, coding, analysis, hypothesis generation, synthesis, and testing alternative specifications.

I think this matters because many research institutions were designed around the assumption that failed scientific attempts are expensive.

At the same time, scientific evaluation remains scarce. Reviewers have limited time, domain expertise is expensive, and AI can increase the amount of scientific output much faster than it increases the number of people able to judge that output.

That has led me to a current question I care about:

If AI makes scientific generation abundant, does judgment become the bottleneck?

I am interested in technical systems for evaluating AI-generated scientific work, including methodological validation, provenance, uncertainty, reproducibility, evidence tracing, and escalation to domain experts.

I wrote a Substack essay synthesizing much of this thinking and tracing the history of scientific infrastructure through the lens of how institutions select uncertain work.

## What I'm looking for

I’m looking for work where I can build real systems, own meaningful technical problems, and work closely with people who care about whether the product actually works in the real world.

I’m especially interested in early-stage teams and technically ambitious environments where the boundary between software engineering, machine learning, product thinking, and research is not rigid.

The problems I am most drawn to involve:

* AI systems that interact with real users or real institutional workflows;
* evaluation and reliability of LLM or agent systems;
* browser and workflow automation where safety and determinism matter;
* scientific and research infrastructure;
* computational health;
* ranking, retrieval, anomaly detection, and decision-support systems;
* tools that improve how people discover information, opportunities, or talent.

I generally prefer problems where there is a concrete user, a real failure mode, and a system that can be tested rather than a purely speculative AI demo.

I am also interested in teams where junior engineers are expected to own substantial pieces of a system instead of only completing isolated tickets.

Longer term, I want to build companies and institutions that change how people make important decisions, pursue scientific work, and use increasingly capable AI systems without giving up human judgment.

## Voice notes (how drafts should sound)

Write in first person.

Be direct, concrete, and specific.

Do not use phrases like:

* "I am passionate about..."
* "I am thrilled..."
* "I am deeply excited..."
* "leveraging cutting-edge technology"
* "at the intersection of..."
* "dynamic environment"
* "innovative solutions"
* "synergy"
* "revolutionize"
* "transformative journey"

Do not use exclamation marks.

Do not use em dashes.

Avoid overly polished corporate language.

Lead with the specific thing I built, researched, measured, shipped, or learned.

Prefer:
"I built..."
"I worked on..."
"I noticed..."
"I started by..."
"I initially thought..."
"The problem was..."
"What interested me was..."
"That changed how I thought about..."
"The part I would want to work on is..."

When describing technical work, include enough implementation detail to make the claim credible. Name the relevant language, framework, modeling approach, dataset, system architecture, or measurable result when it helps.

Do not dump technologies just to sound technical.

Whenever possible, explain why a technical decision mattered.

For example, prefer:

"I used SQLite as the single source of truth because browser automation becomes dangerous when application state can diverge across processes."

over:

"I used TypeScript, Playwright, SQLite, Zod, React, and OpenAI."

Show evidence rather than describing myself with adjectives.

Prefer:

"I built and shipped the iOS app into a live Hopkins pilot with 30+ users."

over:

"I am an entrepreneurial and driven engineer."

Prefer:

"I built the MVP in four days and iterated on it after feedback."

over:

"I work well in fast-paced environments."

It is okay for the writing to sound slightly conversational. It should sound like a technically curious college student who has actually built things, not a professional resume writer.

Avoid one-sentence paragraphs used only for dramatic emphasis.

Use longer, natural paragraphs when explaining a project or motivation.

When discussing a failure or change in thinking, be honest about it. I often learn by starting with a strong hypothesis, testing it against users, technical constraints, or expert feedback, and changing the thesis when it stops making sense.

That intellectual movement is part of my voice.

Do not pretend I have expertise I do not have. I am an undergraduate who has built and researched extensively, not a senior engineer, physician, economist, or professor.

When writing about research, distinguish between:

* what I personally found or built;
* what a paper or expert argued;
* what I currently hypothesize.

When writing application essays, the goal is not to cram every accomplishment into the answer. Pick the 1–3 experiences most directly relevant to the role and explain them clearly.

The strongest recurring themes in my work are:

1. I build systems around real problems I encounter.
2. I care about where automation should stop, not only where it can go.
3. I am interested in evaluation and judgment as AI makes generation cheaper.
4. I repeatedly move between technical implementation and institutional/product questions.
5. I like finding hidden talent, neglected ideas, or information that conventional systems fail to surface.
6. I am willing to change my thesis when reality contradicts it.
7. I care about building things that actually get used.
8. I am unusually interested in the incentives and institutional structures surrounding technology, not only the technology itself.",
